source.title: Large language models encode clinical knowledge
source.authors: K. Singhal; Shekoofeh Azizi; Tao Tu; S. Mahdavi; Jason Wei; Hyung Won Chung; Nathan Scales; A. Tanwani; H. Cole-Lewis; Stephen Pfohl; P. Payne; Martin G. Seneviratne; P. Gamble; Chris Kelly; A. Babiker; Nathanael Schärli; A. Chowdhery; P. A. Mansfield; Dina Demner-Fushman; B. A. Y. Arcas; D. Webster; G. Corrado; Yossi Matias; K. record.tranche_reason: Tests how model size relates to performance on medical question-answering tasks, an applied downstream setting rather than held-out pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The study reports downstream medical QA accuracy across PaLM and Flan-PaLM size variants, which bears on V6. It does not report held-out cross-entropy loss, fit power laws to loss, test small-run loss extrapolation, or study compute-optimal parameter/token allocation or architecture shape. The CoT and self-consistency comparisons are prompting ablations, not scaling results; human-evaluation outcomes do not measure the scaling claim.
record.test_reason: Table 5 reports few-shot accuracy on three medical multiple-choice benchmarks for PaLM and Flan-PaLM at 8B, 62B and 540B. This is a downstream-performance-versus-scale result in a new domain, so it bears on V6. With only three sizes and no fit, loss measure or extrapolation, it shows the direction of the trend, not its predictability. Nothing bears on V1–V5 or V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with two corrections. The roughly 2x gain from 8B to 540B is stated for PaLM and Flan-PaLM, and the authors say it is most pronounced on MedQA and MedMCQA; it is not uniform across all tasks (Flan-PaLM PubMedQA goes only 67.6→79.0). The authors also suggest that strong medical QA may be an emergent ability of scale combined with instruction prompt tuning. Their claim that 'scale alone is insufficient' rests on human evaluation of 540B models only, so it is not a scaling comparison.
record.recipe_differences: Measures downstream medical QA accuracy across model sizes rather than held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss, loss-law fitting, or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported size trends are conditioned on dataset, model family (PaLM or instruction-tuned Flan-PaLM), and few-shot prompt count. The paper also reports prompting ablations, but those are not scaling results.
record.problems: The scaling comparison uses only three model sizes and task accuracy rather than held-out loss; the paper gives no uncertainty estimates for the Table 5 scaling values. PaLM's PubMedQA accuracy is non-monotonic across the reported sizes.
record.rows_left_out: The paper's plotted scaling curves in Appendix Figure A.1 repeat the Table 5 size comparisons and were not added as duplicate rows. CoT/self-consistency results and human evaluations were left out because they do not measure the size-dependent downstream pattern named in V6.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No fits on small runs used to predict larger runs.
No architecture-shape comparisons at fixed parameter count.
No power-law fit in other modalities or training regimes. Instruction tuning is compared only as an accuracy offset, not as a scaling law.

Predictability is not tested: there is no functional fit, no extrapolation, and no relation to pretraining loss. Only three sizes are used, which also differ in compute (Fig A.1 x-axis is FLOPs). MMLU clinical topics, CoT and self-consistency are reported only at 540B in tables.
No exponents or fitting choices compared.

missing.what: Flan-PaLM few-shot+CoT+self-consistency accuracy across model sizes (FLOPs axis) on MedQA and MedMCQA. It is plotted only, with no numbers.

record.verdict_notes: The record's uncertainty_reported 'y' is wrong for the scaling results: Table 5 gives no intervals, and confidence intervals appear only for the human evaluations. The 8B rows were marked 'observed' although they are reference points; they should serve as baselines. The model sizes also differ in compute, since all were trained on 780B tokens, so size and compute effects are confounded, though consistently with V6. The 8B MedQA score near chance hints at an emergence-style jump rather than smooth predictability, which the authors themselves raise.

versions.untested_parts: The study reports downstream QA accuracy, not held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
No power laws are fitted on small runs and evaluated as predictions of larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or loss-minimising parameter/token split is tested.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study evaluates medical QA, but does not test whether the claimed pretraining-loss power law transfers to other modalities or training regimes.
Tests accuracy on selected medical QA benchmarks across three sizes, but not predictability from pretraining loss, extrapolation to larger sizes, or downstream tasks beyond those benchmarks.
No loss exponents or compute-optimal allocation are fitted or compared across setup and fitting choices.

relationships.condition: PaLM and Flan-PaLM, MedQA and MedMCQA, few-shot
relationships.reason: Accuracy rises monotonically 8B→62B→540B: PaLM MedQA 25.7→40.9→58.9, Flan MedMCQA 34.5→46.2→56.5 (r1–r12).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increased monotonically, including PaLM MedQA from 25.7 to 40.9 to 58.9 and Flan-PaLM MedMCQA from 34.5 to 46.2 to 56.5.

relationships.reason: Accuracy rises 67.6→77.2→79.0, but the last gain is small near the cited 78% human ceiling (r16–r18).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increased 67.6→77.2→79.0, with a small final gain near the cited 78% human ceiling.

relationships.reason: Accuracy rises 34.0→57.8 from 8B to 62B, then falls to 55.0 at 540B, so the trend is not monotonic (r13–r15).
relationships.display_finding: On PubMedQA with three-shot prompting, PaLM accuracy rises from 34.0 at 8B to 57.8 at 62B, then falls to 55.0 at 540B.

relationships.reason: The 8B models score near chance (25.7%, 26.7%) and the authors frame the gains as possibly emergent. A smooth, predictable trend from small scale is not shown (r1, r7).
relationships.display_finding: The 8B model scores near chance at 25.7% on MedQA and 26.7% on MedMCQA, with larger-model gains described as potentially emergent.
